title.en: After the Fire: Baldr Returns, the Earth Rises Green
title.zh: 烈焰之後：巴爾德歸返，大地回青

region.en: The risen earth and Idavoll (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 重升的大地與伊達平原（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

summary.en: Ragnarok ends with a harvest-catalog: the earth rises once more from the sea, green and beautiful; waterfalls run; the eagle flies over the mountains hunting fish. The surviving gods meet on Idavoll and find again the golden game-pieces in the grass; fields bear fruit unsown; Baldr and Höd come back; Hoenir works divination; two human beings, Lif and Lifthrasir, are hidden in the wood and feed on morning dew; a hall more bright than the sun stands at Gimle. But the sibyl's last vision is not peace: she sees the dragon flying from the corpse-shore, corpses in its feathers, and sinks away. The record is the Norse doctrine that the end is survivable, the institutions refoundable - and the record of crimes not erasable.
summary.zh: 諸神黃昏以一串豐饒意象作結：大地自海中再度升起，青翠而美麗；瀑布奔流；鷹在山間捕魚飛翔。倖存的神在伊達平原重聚，在草間重新拾起黃金棋子；未經播種的田野自動結果；巴爾德與霍德歸返；海尼爾重掌占卜；一男一女（利夫與利夫特赫拉西爾）藏於林中，以晨露為食；一座比太陽更亮的宮殿立於吉姆萊。然而女先知最後的幻象並非和平：她看見巨龍自屍骸之濱飛出，羽翼間夾帶屍骸，隨即沉入沉眠。此記錄是北歐的教義：終結可以倖存，制度可以重建——而罪惡的記錄無法抹除。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The renewal is staged as an inventory of what comes back. Völuspá's sequence: 'the sun turns black, the earth sinks in the sea, the hot stars fall from the sky, and the fire leaps high about the citadel of the gods' - and then the next stanza turns the page: 'but there will yet arise a green earth from the sea, and waterfalls fall, and the eagle flies that hunts fish on the mountain'. The world's renewal is told in ecological shorthand: green ground, running water, a working food-chain. Vafthrudnismal confirms the detail through Odin's exam: 'unsown fields will bear fruit; all sickness will heal; Baldr will come; Höd and Baldr both settle in Hropt's victory-halls, the gods' dwellings - do you know yet?' - the harvest and the healed body, the returned god and the killer reconciled, in the same breath.

The institutions refound themselves. The surviving gods meet on Idavoll, 'the plain where the gods met before', and there they find in the grass the golden game-pieces the older gods played with - the golden age's board-game recovered by literal rediscovery, the restoration thesis of the whole cycle: institutions can be lost and refound with the selfsame objects. Snorri completes the roster: Vidar and Vali live, neither sea nor Surtr's fire has harmed them; Modi and Magni, Thor's sons, have Mjollnir; Hoenir works prophecy and chooses lots; and 'the sons of Baldr lived and were busy? ' - Baldr and Höd return from Hel to sit in Odin's old seat.

Humanity too is renewed: Lif ('life') and Lifthrasir ('striving-for-life') hide in Hoddmimir's wood, feed on the morning dew, and from them come so many generations that the world is peopled - the remnant-pair doctrine, the same grammar as Bergelmir's raft at creation: every world-epoch begins with one couple saved by geography. And the architecture of the new age is specified: a hall more beautiful than the sun stands at Gimle, roofed with red gold, where righteous people shall live and enjoy pleasure forever; also Brimir's hall at Okolnir, full of good drink; and Nidafjoll, where the dragon Nidhoggr is - and the last lines of the poem fly the dragon from the corpse-shore with corpses in its feathers: the renewal admits no criminals, but neither does it erase the record of crime.

The cultural function is the Norse doctrine of survivable endings. Where most mythologies make the end absolute (the deluge, the flood, the apocalyptic furnace), the Norse eschatology is scheduled, fought, and survived: the gods can lose and the world can go on, because the end is a regime change, not a deletion. Snorri's Gylfaginning closes its catechism with exactly this - the young king's lesson is that the pagan world knew its own mortality and planned beyond it. And the genre's politics are visible: the stanzas are the victory-catalog of what a thirteenth-century Icelander thought irreplaceable - law-courts refound, games recovered, kinship reconciled, harvest, healing, and a hall better than the sun for the righteous.

For the atlas, the record anchors the world-renewal motif family (A-code world renewal, resurrection): the Chinese mulberry-catastrophes' survivors, the Maya's new world-ages, the Zoroastrian renovation at Frashegird - each an after-the-end inventory; the Norse one is unique in making the inventory institutional (game-pieces, courts, halls) and in ending with an unpunished dragon.

functions: Doctrine of survivable endings: Ragnarok as regime change, not deletion
Institutional restoration: law-courts, game-pieces and halls refound with the selfsame objects
Remnant-pair doctrine: humanity renewed from one couple saved by geography
Closure with an unpunished dragon: renewal admits the righteous and outlasts crime

title.en: Lif and Lifthrasir: The Last Couple in the Wood
title.zh: 利夫與利夫特赫拉西爾：林中末世雙親

region.en: Hoddmimir's holt (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 霍德密米爾之林（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

texts.period: Vafthrudnismal st. 45 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Vafthrudnismal st. 45; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 53; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

texts.license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Asked what will remain of humankind when the Fimbulwinter has blown its three winters, the giant answers: a man and a woman, Lif ('life') and Lifthrasir ('striving-for-life'), whose food is the morning dew; they hide in Hoddmimir's holt, and from them come so many kindreds that the world is peopled. Snorri adds the geography: the wood is 'the woman? ' - no - the names map onto Loddlynir's morning food and Yggdrasil's dew; the couple are humanity's remnant-pair, scheduled to outlast the gods themselves.
summary.zh: 當被問及芬布爾之冬連吹三冬之後人類還剩下什麼，巨人答道：一男一女，利夫（「生命」）與利夫特赫拉西爾（「力求生者」），以清晨露水為食；他們藏身於霍德密米爾之林，其後代繁衍至足以重新佈滿世界。斯諾里補充地理細節：那片林子藏於世界樹的晨露之下；這對伴侶是人類的孑遺之偶，注定比諸神本身活得更久。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
In the wisdom-contest of Vafthrudnismal, Odin asks the question that outsizes the rest: 'whence will come the sun to the smooth heaven, when the wolf has swallowed this?' - and then, after the sun is answered, the human question: 'what will remain of the sons of men when the fierce Surt's fire has burned?' The giant answers: 'in Hoddmimir's holt, Lif and Lifthrasir shall hide; the morning dew they have for food; from them the kindreds will come, men beyond number - and it will be a wonder, whence comes the sun, when Fenrir has seized this one.'

Gylfaginning retells the doctrine in its catechism: during the fire of Surtr, two people hide in the wood Hoddmimir's holt, called Lif and Lifthrasir, and their food is the morning dew; and from these two there is so great a kinship of descent that the world is peopled, 'as is here said'. Snorri adds the interpretive gloss that the wood is the morning dew, taken 'in Hoddmimir's holt' as a kenning: the wood is that which 'holds Mimir' - and the Mimir that holds it is Yggdrasil's bark itself, so the last humans survive inside the world-tree's dew. The doctrine is thus a bracket to Ask and Embla: the first humans were made from trees, and the last humans are saved by one.

The record's cultural functions are the doctrine of survivable humanity and the economy of the minimal. Every world-religion has a flood-pair; the Norse version is distinctive for its detail: the couple are named for processes (life, striving-for-life), fed on dew (the world-tree's own moisture - they are not eating stores, they are eating the cosmos's metabolism), and their post-doom multiplication is not a promise but a demographic statement ('kindreds beyond number'). The pairing of gods' mortality with human persistence is the eschatology's sharpest inversion: everything divine is scheduled to fail; the ordinary couple, hidden in wood, outlasts Odin.

In the atlas, the record anchors the remnant-couple family (Deucalion and Pyrrha; Utnapishtim; the Chinese brother-sister pair after the flood): each tradition's minimal humanity; the Norse one is characterized by dew, wood, and names that are processes rather than persons.

The couple's names complete the doctrine: Lif ('life') and Lifthrasir ('striving-for-life') are processes rather than persons - the remnant-pair named for what they do, not who they are - and their food (the morning dew of Hoddmimir's holt, the world-tree's own moisture) makes them eaters of the cosmos's metabolism rather than of stores. And the bracket completes the record: the first humans made from trees (Ask and Embla) and the last humans saved by one (the holt) - the wood that animated the species at the beginning shelters it at the end, the myth's own bookends. The record thus anchors the remnant-couple family: humanity's minimal pair surviving the gods' end, distinctive in dew, wood and process-names.

functions: Remnant-couple doctrine: humanity renewed from one pair saved by geography
Bracket to Ask and Embla: the first humans made from trees, the last saved by one
Dew-economy of survival: the couple live on the world-tree's own moisture
Inversion of divine mortality: the ordinary couple outlasts the gods

title.en: Gimle: The Hall Brighter Than the Sun
title.zh: 吉姆萊：比太陽更亮的宮殿

region.en: Gimle, the southern heaven (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 吉姆萊，南方天穹（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

texts.period: Voluspa st. 64-65 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

summary.en: At the end of the sibyl's vision she sees a hall 'more beautiful than the sun' standing at Gimle, roofed with red gold, where the righteous people shall live and enjoy delight forever. Snorri adds the rest of the new sky's real estate: another hall at Okolnir, Brimir's, full of good drink, for the honest folk; a third on Nidafjoll, red gold, 'Nastrand's'; and above the sky itself, Andlang and Vidblainn, where nothing unclean may live. The record is the Norse post-doom geography: heaven with zoning by purity.
summary.zh: 女先知幻象終結之時，她看見一座「比太陽更美」的宮殿立於吉姆萊，屋頂覆以紅金，正直之人將在此永享歡愉。斯諾里補充新天穹的其餘產業：另一座在奧科爾尼爾，名為布利米爾之廳，盛滿美酒，為誠實者所居；第三座位於尼達山，紅金蓋頂，「屬納斯特隆德」；而天穹之上還有安蘭與維德布拉因，凡不潔之物皆不得居於其中。此記錄是北歐末日之後的地理：以純潔分區的天堂。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The sibyl's renewal-vision ends in real estate: 'there may the righteous people live, and forever enjoy delight' - in a hall more beautiful than the sun, roofed with red gold, at Gimle ('fire-shelter', from the same root as the shelter from Muspell's fire). Gylfaginning expands the catalog into a doctrine: besides Gimle, Brimir's hall at Okolnir ('the never-cold'), full of good drink, for those 'who are honest'; a third hall on Nidafjoll, 'red gold, which is called Nastrand', whose inmates are the sworn oath-breakers and murderers - the punishment-hall's address in the renewed world; and above Gimle, above even that, Andlang ('the stretched-wide') and Vidblainn ('the wide-blue'), where 'no unrighteous thing can live' - the outermost heaven, purer still, which protects the renewed world from Niflhel's cold and Muspell's fire.

The record's cultural function is the zoning of the after-doom world by purity and dessert. Gimle is the reward-hall for 'the righteous' (the poem says 'godhirlifor men' - men living well); Brimir's hall is the compensation for honest but unrighteous? - the honest get beer, the righteous get gold and light; and Nastrand remains the doom-hall of the oath-breakers, whose river of knives flows on even in the renewed world. The purity-doctrine extends upward: nothing unclean lives in Andlang and Vidblainn - a doctrine that reads like Christian influence, and editors have long argued whether these stanzas are native or borrowed from Revelation's new heaven; Snorri's systematization, which both preserves the native halls and adds the purity-zones, is the learned medieval synthesis in action.

For the atlas, Gimle anchors the post-apocalyptic heaven family: the Zoroastrian Best Existence at Frashegird, the Chinese land of mulberry-fields renewed, the Christian new Jerusalem - each an after-the-end paradise; the Norse one is characterized by named halls, gold roofs, and zoning by honesty.

The comparative frame completes the doctrine: the Zoroastrian Best Existence at Frashegird, the Christian new Jerusalem and the Chinese renewed mulberry-fields are the renewal-paradise family - each an after-the-end heaven with named architecture; the Norse one is distinctive in its zoning (righteous, honest, oath-breaking) and in its endurance of the punishment-hall inside the renewed world. And the purity-doctrine's upper registers (Andlang and Vidblainn, where nothing unclean lives) show the learned synthesis at work: the medieval compiler's reconciliation of the poem's renewal-halls with a Christian-flavored stratified heaven - the record's critical datum is that the synthesis itself is documented, the old halls and the new purity-zones coexisting in Snorri's chapter.

functions: Post-doom heaven with zoning: the righteous at Gimle, the honest at Brimir's hall, oath-breakers retained at Nastrand
Purity-doctrine of the outer heavens: nothing unclean in Andlang and Vidblainn
Real-estate eschatology: the renewed world's halls named, roofed and occupied
Comparative anchor of the post-apocalyptic paradise family

title.en: Gylfaginning: King Gylfi, the Three Teachers and the Illusion of Asgard
title.zh: 《居爾菲的幻惑》：居爾菲王、三重講席與阿斯加德的幻象

region.en: The road to Asgard from Sweden (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 自瑞典通往阿斯加德的路（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

texts.period: Prose Edda c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to (c. 1300-1325), Codex Upsaliensis DG 11, Codex Trajectinus

source.work: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Gylfaginning chs. 1-3, 53; critical ed. Anthony Faulkes (1987)

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Edda's mythic textbook is staged as a trick: King Gylfi of Sweden, having given a wandering woman (Gefjon) a ploughland, seeks the Aesir's wisdom; he travels to Asgard under the name Gangleri, finds a palace where three enthroned men - High, Just-as-High, Third - answer his catechism on creation, gods, and Ragnarok. When the teaching is done, the palace and its lords vanish, the field is empty, and Gylfi walks home empty-handed. Snorri's frame is a Christian scholar's safety device: the whole pagan mythology is presented as the illusion it is said to be, preserved for skaldic craft, transmitted through a king who was fooled.
summary.zh: 《埃達》的神話教科書以一場幻術呈現：瑞典王居爾菲在賜予流浪女子（格芙永）一片犁地之後，欲尋求阿薩神族的智慧；他化名岡格雷利前往阿斯加德，在宮殿中見到三位端坐的王——「至高者」「同等至高者」「第三者」——以問答方式講授創世、諸神與諸神黃昏。教學完畢，宮殿與王者消失，原野空無一人，居爾菲空手而歸。斯諾里的框架是基督教學者的安全裝置：整個異教神話以「幻象」自居，為吟遊詩藝而保存，經由一位被愚弄的國王傳承。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning - 'the tricking of Gylfi' - is the most consequential frame-story in Norse literature, because it is the container of the entire mythic textbook. The prose begins in Snorri's prologue: the Aesir were human chiefs out of Asia (Tyrkland) who migrated north, bringing crafts and cult; their wisdom was mistaken for divinity. Then the frame: King Gylfi, ruler of 'the land that is now called Sweden', once granted a wandering woman as much land as four oxen could plough in a day and a night - and she turned out to be the goddess Gefjon, whose four ox-sons ploughed Zealand out of his kingdom. Angry, or curious, Gylfi determined to seek the Aesir and learn whether their power was of their own nature or of craft. Under the assumed name Gangleri ('the weary traveler'), he sets out for Asgard.

The catechism is the Edda's body. In a great hall Gylfi meets three enthroned figures - the highest named Hár (High), the middle Jafnhár (Equal-high), the third Thridi (Third) - and asks, in the manner of a catechumen: 'who is the highest and most ancient of all gods? what was the beginning? how was the earth made? what of the sun and moon? the Norns? the gods' dwellings? the deaths of Baldr, of Thor, of Odin? what comes after?' - and each question is answered from the poems: Gylfaginning is a prose exegesis that quotes Voluspa, Vafthrudnismal, Grimnismal as scripture. The three answers are marked by the refrain 'so it is said' - and the whole is delivered as something told, not believed.

The frame's punchline is the trick's exposure. When the teaching is done and Gylfi has heard of the renewal after Ragnarok, he looks around - and sees no hall and no lords: the place is open country. 'Gangleri saw around him a great plain, and no hall and no stronghold; he went his way and came to his kingdom, and told what he had seen and heard.' The three teachers were the three Aesir (Odin among them?) showing a king 'an illusion of the great power that they had'. Snorri's stated purpose, in the prologue to Skaldskaparmal, is that these stories are preserved 'for the needs of poetry' - to teach the kenning-system to young skalds - so the illusion-frame is also a quarantine: the myths may be used as language, not as doctrine.

The record's cultural functions are the learned-Christian quarantine and the pedagogy of deception. Iceland converted in 1000 CE but kept its verse; Snorri, writing two centuries later under a church that burned heretics elsewhere in Europe, needed a container that let him explain Thor's fishing and Odin's runes without endorsing them - the answer was a frame that defines the myths as illusion, quotes them as sources, and licenses them as craft. The result is the single most important document of the myth corpus: without Gylfaginning's catechism, most of the Edda's mythology would exist only in fragmentary verse; with it, the myths survive in narrative form - preserved by a Christian's irony, which is itself a critical fact for the digital historian.

For the atlas, the record anchors the frame-trick family: the Chinese 'Yellow Emperor's dialogues', the Persian Bundahishn's schoolroom of Ohrmazd, the Christian catechism itself - each a container-story; Snorri's is distinctive in making the container dissolve at the end, leaving the reader with the myths and no teacher.

functions: Quarantine-frame: pagan myth presented as learned illusion, licensed only as poetic craft
Pedagogy by catechism: creation to Ragnarok answered by three enthroned teachers
Prose exegesis quoting eddic verse as scripture - the myths' survival strategy
Dissolving container: the teacher vanishes, leaving the reader with the stories

passages.text: King Gylfi ruled the land that is now called Sweden; wise and skilled in magic, he marveled that the Aesir-people knew all things better than others. He took the name Gangleri and made ready his journey to Asgard, that he might learn whether their power was of their own nature or of craft.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 2 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the great hall he saw three enthroned men: the first named High, the second Equal-high, the third Third. And each of his questions - of the beginning of the world, the sun and moon, the gods' dwellings, Baldr's death, the doom to come - they answered from the old poems, saying 'so it is said'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 2-3 and passim (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when the teaching was done, Gangleri looked about him and saw a great plain, no hall and no stronghold; he went his way and came to his kingdom, and told what he had seen and heard. And the Aesir took counsel and agreed to send three figures to answer him - an illusion of the great power they seemed to have.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 53 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Eiriksmal: Valhalla Prepares for a Dead King
title.zh: 《埃里克之歌》：瓦爾哈拉為亡王備宴

region.en: Valhalla's gates (symbolic pin at York, England - Eirik's last battle?)
region.zh: 瓦爾哈拉之門（象徵性定位於英格蘭約克——埃里克的末戰之地？）

texts.period: c. 954 CE (for the death of Eirik Bloodaxe); quoted in Fagrskinna and Snorri's Edda; text in Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883)

source.archive: Skaldic Poetry of the Scandinavian Middle Ages / Corpus Poeticum Boreale

texts.license: Public domain (CPB 1883); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Composed for the death of Eirik Bloodaxe (c. 954), this skaldic poem is the earliest surviving vision of Valhalla from inside: the gods wake in Valhalla asking why the day is darkened and what the din of arms means; Bragi answers that Odin has bidden Eirik with his host to come up. Sigmund rises to bid the king welcome and asks the poem's great joke: why should Odin take Eirik, a king who might have lived, when the gods could have taken famous kings grown old? Odin answers: 'Grey-haired are the gods... the wolf howls at the gates' - and the einherjar brew ale for the king's coming. The record documents the hall as a working, political institution, and a court-poet's craft of consoling a dynasty by drafting its dead king into Odin's army.
summary.zh: 此吟遊詩為埃里克·血斧之死（約954年）而作，是現存最早的「自內部」所見瓦爾哈拉幻象：瓦爾哈拉中的諸神醒來，問白日為何昏暗、兵器之聲為何嘈雜；布拉基答道，奧丁已召埃里克及其部屬前來。西格蒙德起身迎接國王，並問出詩中著名的調侃：神王何以要帶走本可長壽的埃里克，而不帶走那些已功成名就的年老君王？奧丁答：「諸神業已蒼老……狼在門外嗥叫」——恩赫里亞為王之來臨釀酒備宴。此記錄將瓦爾哈拉描繪為一個運作中、具政治性的機構，亦展示宮廷詩人如何透過將亡王編入奧丁軍團來撫慰王族。

texts.canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris, Oxford 1883 (public domain); quoted in Fagrskinna

narrative.en:
Eiriksmal ('the lay of Eirik') is the earliest skaldic poem that opens the door of Valhalla and looks in. Its dramatic frame: the gods wake from sleep and ask 'what nightmare is this? why is the day darkened and the earth trembling? what din is this, as if hosts were coming?' - Bragi answers that the din is the coming of the dead king: 'the All-father has bidden Eirik, the sea-king, to come up with his host to Odin's halls.' Sigmund, leader of the chosen, rises to greet him: 'why hast thou taken Eirik from the lands rather than other kings, that thy hand should make the battle-beaten king come into Odin's hall?' 

Odin's answer is the poem's doctrine compressed: 'Grey-haired are the gods, and grown old? - the einherjar are few? ' - no; the verse reads: 'Grey-haired are the gods and few the chosen; the wolf howls at the gates; grey-headed they gather for the wolf's attack; I have gotten me Eirik, whom I had rather? ' - the point is demographic: Valhalla needs recruits against Ragnarok, and the All-father drafts the best of the battle-slain by preference. Then the hall prepares the feast: 'Ale for Eirik is brewed in Valhalla; the vessel with the rim? is rinsed; the warriors chosen; the shield-wood (targets) laid; we await Eirik.' The poem ends with the welcome at the doors.

The record's cultural functions are threefold. First, it documents the myth-as-institution: the hall has a census, a recruitment policy, kitchen preparations and a door-protocol - the afterlife as a functioning barracks, not a metaphor. Second, it is court politics in mythic dress: the poem was composed for Eirik's dynasty (his widow Gunnhildr's court), and its joke - Sigmund asking why the gods take a useful king - is the consolation-argument of a court poet to a royal widow: your husband was too valuable to die of disease; the gods wanted him. Third, it is documentary evidence for the Norse doctrine that kings are drafted: the dead king's afterlife career is a conscription, and the poem's performance at court converted mourning into enlistment news.

Its companion, Hakonarmal (Eyvindr skaldaspillir, c. 961, for Hakon the Good - a Christian-leaning king!), does the same work and even has Odin send the valkyries down to choose the king alive; taken together the two poems are the best documentation of Valhalla's ideological work in tenth-century court culture. In the atlas, the record anchors the chosen-death and royal-drafting motif family, answering the Chinese astral promotion of dead officials and the Islamic martyrdom doctrine - each a death-to-office pipeline; the Norse one runs through a barracks with a welcome-committee.

functions: Valhalla as institution: census, recruitment policy, kitchen and door-protocol
Court politics in mythic dress: consolation of a royal widow by mythic conscription
Doctrine of the royal draft: kings taken by preference for the army of Ragnarok
Earliest inside-view of the hall, documented by court poetry (c. 954)

title.en: Hel-shoes: Shoeing the Dead for the Road to Hel
title.zh: 冥途鞋：為亡者穿上走向海爾的鞋

region.en: Skagafjordur, Iceland (burial custom attested in Kormaks saga)
region.zh: 冰島斯卡加峽灣（科爾馬克薩迦所載葬俗）

texts.period: Kormaks saga 13th century (custom of older origin); Landnamabok attestation; principal MSS of the sagas 13th-14th c.

source.work: Kormaks saga ch. 22 (the hel-shoes for the dead); Landnamabok; ed. Islenzk Fornrit VIII (1939)

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: A unique Icelandic custom is documented in the sagas: 'hel-shoes' were made for the dead. In Kormaks saga, a man dies; when his kinsmen find him, they shoe him for the road, and the saga explains the custom: shoes were made for dead men so that they might walk to Hel - for there is a district in Hel where shoes are put out for guests, and he that arrives without shoes must wade through mire. The record is the Norse aition of grave-goods-as-clothing: the underworld has a hospitality economy, and footwear is its entrance fee.
summary.zh: 冰島薩迦記載了一項獨特的習俗：為死者製作「冥途鞋」（hel-skór）。在《科爾馬克薩迦》中，有人死去；親屬尋見其屍，為其穿鞋上路；薩迦並解釋此俗：為亡者製鞋，使其得以步行至海爾之境——因冥府中有一處專為賓客備鞋之地，無鞋而至者必須蹚過泥沼。此記錄是北歐「隨葬品即衣物」的起源故事：冥府有其待客經濟，鞋履便是入門的通行費。

texts.canonical_translation: Kormaks saga, Islenzk Fornrit VIII, Reykjavik 1939; paraphrase

narrative.en:
Kormaks saga, a poet's saga of the 10th century set down in the 13th, contains one of the most striking ritual doctrines in the corpus: when Kormak's enemy Bersi is found dead (killed by Kormak's shield-kin? - by Kormak's riddling duel), the account runs: 'they shoe him'? - the saga says that when a man died, shoes were made for him, 'and that is called hel-shoes' (helskó). The doctrine that explains the custom is given as a proverb of the dead: there is a district in Hel called the shoe-parish (Skó? - the saga's phrasing is 'there is a place in Hel where they put out shoes for guests'), and he that arrives unshod must wade through mire the whole way; hence shoes were made for the dead 'and this they call hel-shoes, and it is a service rendered? ' - the custom is meritorious, an act of hospitality extended to the dead kinsman for his journey.

Landnamabok, the settlement-book, confirms the custom's currency in early Iceland: its phrase 'and they had hel-shoes made for him' recurs in its death-notices, indicating the practice was normative rather than anecdotal. Archaeologically, shoes in graves are documented (children's shoes in Christian-era cemeteries, which some scholars connect with the doctrine's persistence after conversion); the custom belongs to the wider grave-goods economy - weapons for warriors, ships' fittings for sailors? - and this record documents its most mundane and most tender form: shoes for a walk of nine nights.

The cultural functions are the underworld's hospitality economy and the doctrine of provision. The image of Hel as a place with guest-services (a district where shoes are put out for guests) domesticates the afterlife: death's journey is a visit, and the living owe the dead traveler the same provisioning as any guest - shoes at the door, as one leaves for a road. And the custom's persistence after conversion (the saga records it as still intelligible in Christian times) shows how a death-geography survives its theology: even where the destination changed, the provision of shoes kept its meaning.

In the atlas, the record anchors the provision-for-the-dead family: the Chinese paper offerings burned for the dead, the Egyptian ushabti servants, the Greek obol for the ferryman - each a traveler's kit for the underworld; the Norse one is unique in being footwear, and in naming the alternative (wading through mire) rather than a toll.

The custom's archaeology completes the doctrine: shoes recovered from Christian-era Icelandic cemeteries (the children's shoes of the churchyards) document the practice's persistence after conversion - the provision kept when the destination changed. And the doctrine's geography completes the record: Hel's shoe-district (the saga's hospitable parish of the dead) domesticates the underworld - death's journey is a visit, and the living owe the dead traveler guest-service, shoes at the door as for any departing kinsman. The record thus anchors the provision-for-the-dead family: the north's own traveler's kit for the road to Hel, distinctive in being footwear and in naming the alternative (the mire) rather than a toll.

functions: Aition of grave-shoes: footwear as entrance provision for the road to Hel
Underworld hospitality economy: a district in Hel puts out shoes for guests
Doctrine of provision: the living owe the dead traveler guest-service
Custom's persistence after conversion: death-geography outliving its theology
